core.title: Keep the package manager's native lockfile as the only lockfile
core.given: A workspace that declares its package manager (the choice is declared, independent of which lockfiles currently exist), with scan roots outside the excluded trees
core.when: the scanned tree holds a foreign lockfile (a lockfile written by a package manager other than the declared one), committed or not, or the current change adds or changes a dependency
core.then: Keep the declared package manager's native lockfile as the single dependency-resolution source: remove every foreign lockfile; none may sit alongside the native lockfile.
prefer: During GREEN: if the current change adds a dependency, install it with the declared package manager.
During GREEN: remove only foreign lockfiles; regenerate the native lockfile only when dependency state actually changed; keep package-manager behavior otherwise untouched.
avoid: Keeping a second lockfile as a temporary convenience, including during a migration window.
Suppressing the finding for a package deliberately not on the declared package manager; it stays reported until it moves to the declared package manager or out of the scanned tree.
unless: A vendored or fixture lockfile inside an excluded tree is never scanned.
core.why: Two lockfiles mean two resolvers disagree about the dependency graph; whichever command a developer or CI step runs wins. Two lockfiles can pin different versions of the same transitive dependency, so the installed tree depends on which tool ran last (resolution drift), and this is invisible in review because nobody reads a lockfile diff — the 'works on my machine, breaks in CI' failure. Risk peaks while migrating to the declared package manager: the old lockfile is still committed, someone runs the old package manager's install command out of habit, the trees fork, and a deploy fails much later. The rule matters more during a migration than after one.
evidence: The current behavioral acceptance and the install/check path pass.
No foreign lockfile exists in the declared scan roots; only the native lockfile governs dependency resolution.
The stack's single-lockfile check reports zero foreign-lockfile findings.
verification: Strict disposition: fails on every finding; no advisory mode, no ratchet baseline. Severity 3.

The check walks the declared scan roots and matches foreign lockfile basenames (resolution records written by a package manager that is not the stack's), regardless of version-control status (committed or not).
Each foreign lockfile is reported at line 1: the file itself is the fact, so there is no line to point at.

No per-rule scope: a package deliberately not on the declared package manager stays reported while it sits inside the scanned tree; the finding is the stack decision's open item, not something to suppress.

Lockfile presence alone is not proof of the package-manager choice; activation relies on the workspace declaration. An agent's intent to run a particular install command is not observable; only the resulting diff is.

fires: In a workspace that declares its package manager, a foreign lockfile exists in a non-excluded scan root (committed or uncommitted).
In a workspace that declares its package manager, the current change adds or changes a dependency in the dependency manifest.
A repository declared on a package manager while migrating to it still has its old lockfile present.
A package deliberately not on the declared package manager has its own foreign lockfile inside the scanned tree.
doesNotFire: A vendored or fixture lockfile inside an excluded tree.
A workspace whose only lockfile is the native lockfile and whose current change adds or changes no dependency.
A repository that does not declare the package manager of this stack.

neutralityNotes: The whole convention is stack-mechanical; its neutral core is 'the declared package manager's native lockfile is the single dependency-resolution source; no foreign lockfile coexists'. All concrete names (Bun, bun.lock/bun.lockb, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml/.yml, package.json, npm install, excluded trees, atdd-bun) come from profile keys. The Bun workspace-declaration activation fact (`layer: atdd.workspace.bun`) has no fact kind in the core activation vocabulary, so the declaration scope is expressed in given/fires/doesNotFire plus tooling.workspace_declaration. Detector identity (bun_fullstack_detector) and Bun-specific task terms are bunOnly.
